rot.bishopPair.ideia.samisch.e1: Attack: let us think from White's side, in the Nimzo-Indian Defence, Sämisch Variation. On move four, Black traded the bishop on b4 for the knight on c3, and White was left with doubled pawns on c3 and c4.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.samisch.e2: In return, White kept both bishops, on c1 and d3; Black has one bishop and two knights. When only one side has both bishops, we say it has the bishop pair.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.samisch.l1: The pawn goes to f4 and prepares the advance to f5, to open the position. In an open position, with few blocked pawns, the diagonals are free for the bishops.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.samisch.l2: Defence: Black answers with the pawn to f5 and stops the advance. In a closed position, with the pawns blocked against each other, the knights play better, because they jump over them.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.samisch.l3: In positions like this, the side with the bishop pair tries to open the position, and the side with the knights tries to close it. The position decides which piece is worth more.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.e1: Attack: now with White, in the game ya73 vs timbouktou, Lichess 2024. White has the bishop pair, on d3 and g3; Black has one bishop and two knights.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.e2: The diagonals of both bishops are open. The bishop on g3 already controls b8 and c7, next to the black king.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.p: Find the move in which the two bishops give mate together.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.certo: The bishop captures the pawn on a6 with check and mate.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.revela: The bishop on d3 captures the pawn on a6 with check and mate. The bishop on g3 controls b8 and c7, and the one on a6 controls b7: the king has no square.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.err.e4d6.1: The knight goes to d6 and gives check, but it stands in the middle of the diagonal of the bishop on g3 to b8.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.err.e4d6.2: The king escapes to b8, and Black has a decisive advantage.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.err.e4d6.3: Back to the position: keep the diagonal of the bishop on g3 free and look for the check of the other bishop.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.fora: That move does not use the bishops. Play one of them.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.volta: Try again: look for the check that leaves the king without a square.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.l0: On a6, the bishop gives mate: each bishop controls squares of one colour around the king.
rot.bishopPair.ideia.dois.l1: In open positions like this, the two bishops together control squares of both colours. A bishop alone only reaches the squares of its own colour.
rot.bishopPair.demos.regra.1: Attack demonstration: now with Black, in the game Creaps vs kajiya, Lichess 2016. Black has the bishop pair, on d6 and e4; White has one bishop and one knight.
rot.bishopPair.demos.regra.2: The bishop on e4 controls the light squares b1 and c2, next to the white king. The bishop on d6 has a free diagonal to a3, where a pawn stands defended by the pawn on b2.
rot.bishopPair.demos.regra.l.3: The queen goes to c3 and gives check: Black gives up the queen to pull the pawn on b2 away.
rot.bishopPair.demos.regra.l.4: The pawn captures the queen: it is the only move, because the bishop on e4 controls b1.
rot.bishopPair.demos.regra.l.5: The bishop captures the pawn on a3 with mate: it controls b2, a dark square, and the bishop on e4 controls b1 and c2, light squares.
rot.bishopPair.demos.regra.l.6: In positions like this, with open diagonals, the bishop pair covers the squares of both colours around the king. A bishop and a knight cannot do that from so far away.
rot.bishopPair.demos.aberta.1: Attack demonstration: again with Black, in the game gio95 vs SergeyDorofeev, Lichess 2018. The black bishop on c6 faces the white knight on a2, with pawns on both wings.
rot.bishopPair.demos.aberta.2: The position is open: the bishop's diagonals are free. The knight on a2, on the edge, reaches few squares.
rot.bishopPair.demos.aberta.l.3: The bishop goes to d5 and gives check. On the same diagonal, behind the king, stands the knight on a2: it is a skewer.
rot.bishopPair.demos.aberta.l.4: The king gets out of check. It cannot go to b3, which is on the bishop's diagonal, and the knight on a2 is still undefended.
rot.bishopPair.demos.aberta.l.5: The bishop captures the knight on a2. From d5, it attacked the king and the knight at the same time, from far away.
rot.bishopPair.demos.aberta.l.6: In positions like this, open and with pawns on both wings, the bishop is worth more than the knight: it plays from far away, and the knight needs several moves to change wings.
rot.bishopPair.demos.excecao.1: Attack demonstration: now with White, in the game ars54321 vs hetraie, Lichess 2016. The knight on d5 stands on an outpost: the pawn on e4 defends it, and no black pawn can drive it away.
rot.bishopPair.demos.excecao.2: The black bishop on g7 moves on the dark squares, like the black pawns on d6 and e5: it is a bad bishop. The centre is closed, with the pawns on e4 and e5 blocked.
rot.bishopPair.demos.excecao.l.3: The knight jumps to e7 and gives check and mate.
rot.bishopPair.demos.excecao.l.4: The queen on f7 cannot capture the knight: the queen on e6 pins it to the king. The rook on h1 takes away h7 and h8. The bad bishop on g7 does not reach e7, and the pawn on e5 closes its diagonal.
rot.bishopPair.demos.excecao.l.5: In positions like this, closed and with an outpost, the knight is worth more than the bad bishop. Trading the knight on d5 for that bishop would throw away the piece that gave mate.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.par.enunciado: Game Mohammedomarat vs winfel, Lichess 2025. You have the bishop pair, and the diagonals are open. Play as White and open the way for the two bishops to give mate.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.par.fim: The queen was given up on c6 to pull the pawn on b7 out of the way. The bishop on a6 gave mate, and the bishop on f4 controlled b8 and c7.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.par.err.f3e3: 18.Qe3? takes the queen away from h1 and g2: after 18...Qh1+ 19.Ke2 Qxg2, Black has a decisive advantage.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.par.err.f3g3: 18.Qg3? retreats the queen and threatens nothing: after 18...Qf5, Black has a decisive advantage.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.par.err.f3h5: 18.Qxh5? trades queens, and the attack is over: after 18...Rxh5, Black, a pawn up, has a decisive advantage.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.aberta.enunciado: Game SpeedrunChess12345 vs milad97, Lichess 2021. The position is open, and your bishop faces a knight. Play as White and use the bishop's range.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.aberta.fim: The bishop gave check from d6 and, at the same time, attacked the rook on h2, on the other side of the board. A knight does not reach two squares so far apart.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.aberta.err.c5f8: 26.Bf8? attacks the pawn on g7, but not the rook: after 26...Rh3+, Black keeps the extra pawns and has a decisive advantage.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.aberta.err.d1d8: 26.Rd8+? gives check, but after 26...Kc7 the king attacks the rook, and Black has a decisive advantage.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.valeAqui.enunciad: Game bobbyjoe44445 vs SaintLouisChessClub, Lichess 2022. Your knight on f4 stands on an outpost, and the white bishop on d3 is bad. Is it worth trading the knight for the bishop here? Play as Black and find the best move.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.valeAqui.fim: The knight gave mate on g2. The bad bishop on d3 does not reach that square, the rook on b2 takes the second rank from the king, and the pawn on e5 takes d4 and f4. Trading the knight for the bishop would throw away the stronger piece.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.valeAqui.err.f4d3: 59...Nxd3? trades the outpost knight for the bad bishop: after 60.Kxd3, the position is equal.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.valeAqui.err.b2b6: 59...Rb6? takes the rook off the second rank: after 60.Bf1, the position is equal.
rot.bishopPair.pratica.valeAqui.err.g6g5: 59...g5? threatens nothing: after 60.Bf1, the bishop protects g2, and the position is equal.
